en: *New Collection of Rituals for Bathing the Image*, one fascicle, composed by Huilin.
The monastic communities of the five regions of India in the Western Regions maintain their practices with somewhat greater solemnity and splendor; some reside in *vihāras*.
In the temples, hermitages, and monastic gardens,
they bathe the images daily, burn incense, gather various famous flowers,
scatter them as offerings, and perform prostrations and praises to the Buddha.
With sincere devotion and reverence,
they circumambulated [the image] every day in this manner,
persevering with diligence until the end of their lives without ceasing.
Every morning at dawn, one must not eat unless this offering has been performed;
throughout distant and near lands, there is no place where this is not practiced.
Indeed, it is that which the assembly of monks constantly cultivates and reverently observes.
As for images, those made of earth, wood, or painted with colors cannot be bathed;
however, images made of gold, silver, precious gems, copper, tin, brass, or similar materials are all suitable for regular bathing.
Regarding the perfumed water to be used for bathing the image tomorrow morning:
tonight, each type of incense should be separately soaked, finely pounded, and wrapped in silk to soak overnight.
Any kind of incense whatsoever is suitable for bathing the image.
Each type of single-flavored scented water should be placed in its own separate bottle;
one should not mix many different fragrances together in a single vessel.
It is best to use bottles that have not been touched by others.
This refers to vessels made of gold, silver, various precious gems, iron, copper, lead, tin, or pure white porcelain that are free from cracks or damage.
All must be polished and washed until they are bright and clean.
The aforementioned sequence for using the names of perfumes as a wheel may be employed.
If one is poor and lacks these, one may take a new, clean vessel made of stone, tile, or wood that has never been used before to serve this purpose.
One must not further use it for other purposes, as this would render it defiled.
Once one has received the perfumed water used for bathing the image and finished using it,
the practitioner of this rite shall maintain pure conduct and guard their deportment.
One must apply extremely refined and meticulous attention;
all ritual implements for offerings should be understood accordingly.
Upon reaching the time for the ablution, one should sprinkle and sweep the hall and the temple.
In a spacious and pure location, smear a large mandala measuring one zhang in diameter with pure cow dung.
Place a preaching platform in the center of the mandala,
and upon it, set a large vessel.
In the center, place a single altar upon which an image of the Honored One is installed; beside it, set a bed.
Cover it with an oil-silk cloth, and arrange various incense burners and water jars in successive rows.
Also prepare the five kinds of Dharma-offerings.
A hundred cords, long threads, new and clean soft silks, bricks, and other such items were arranged upon it.
Once the assembly had gathered,
they together invited the Vidyādhara Ācārya.

Alternatively, the most venerable elder among the assembly shall recite for the multitude the sublime verses of the Mahāyāna from the *Bathing the Image Sūtra* (Snāna-sūtra), which consist of petitions and aspirations;
every member of the assembly shall then follow along in reciting each verse, as follows:
I now bathe all the Tathāgatas—this assembly adorned with the merit of pure wisdom.
May the multitudes of sentient beings in the five turbidities swiftly realize the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body.
May the fragrance of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation pervade the lands of the ten directions, forever diffusing its sweet scent.
May this fragrant smoke likewise perform the work of a Buddha, Immeasurable and boundless,
bringing rest to the wheel of suffering in the three miserable realms; May it universally cause all to eliminate their fever and attain coolness,
To give rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, And to emerge from the river of craving to reach the other shore.
Furthermore, have one person hold an incense burner and kneel with devout reverence,
chanting the Praise of the Three Refuges in a pure, resonant voice (*brahmasvara*).
At the end of each line, the assembly shall perform one prostration.

The praise is as follows: *Namo buddhāya arave* (1); *namo dharmāya dāyine* (2); *namo saṃghāya mahate* (3); *namas tīrthibhyo bhisattvānām* (4). Furthermore, have two people blow conch shells and two people recite this praise.
Various elegant musical instruments—strings, flutes, and vocal songs—were performed all at once.
The Ācārya personally held the water flask and poured water over the Buddha image;
he then took one end of the long cord, tied it to the flask, and let it hang down.
Everyone in the assembly held the thread with both hands, palms joined at the heart,
and recited the names of the Buddhas with single-minded devotion.
Those who were unable to hold the thread did so by joining their palms.
One may take the robes previously worn by the person and hold them;
the intention is as if one were personally bathing each image of the Buddha oneself.
This continues until the water from the incense bottle has been poured out completely in succession once over.
They must be replaced immediately.
Once the bathing is finished, the Buddha images should be reinstalled;
as for those that have not yet been bathed, they should remain as they are.
Furthermore, add the respective types of scented water for each as before and perform the ritual ablution.
Continue blowing the conch, reciting praises, and playing musical instruments until the bathing is complete;
only then should all the honored images be temporarily set aside.
Having rinsed them clean,
he then wiped them dry with a pure cloth and placed them on the bed,
arranged in rows according to their positions.
Then, taking the fragrant unguent, each person should dip their ring finger into it and hold the finger upright at the heart.
The Ācārya recites the mantra for offering the fragrant unguent.
Recite each line with everyone chanting in unison until the final line; then,
all at once, facing the Buddha from afar, offer this by snapping the fingers and perform one prostration.
The mantra for offering scented ointment (*vilepana*) is:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatagandhapūjāmoghasamudra hūṃ. Then, take up the flower tray.
The practitioner and the assembly each hold a flower as before and recite the Flower Offering Mantra in unison.
Facing the Buddha from afar, they scatter the flowers while reciting the Flower Offering Mantra, which says:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāmeghānabhyudgata-spharaṇa-maye hūṃ. Next, the ācārya takes up the incense burner.
Instruct those on his left and right, as well as the assembly,
to hold their robes against one another and recite the incense-burning mantra together, universally offering it with a sincere heart.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatadūṣyapūjāmeghasamudraspharaṇaniścite hūṃ. Furthermore, the ācārya holds a tray of sweet and crisp cakes.
Recite the mantra for offering food as before and present it with a sincere heart.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatābhyo me karmadharaspharaṇi svāhā hūṃ. Next, holding the candle stand, recite the lamp-offering mantra once. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ sarvatathāgatānīti-sarvavid-bhūja-megha-kumāra-spharaṇa-ni-maye hūṃ. Furthermore, have them recite the hymn of praise.
Holding an incense burner in his hand, he recited the "Elegant Praise for Bathing the Image" in a loud voice.
As the text of this praise is extensive and cannot be recorded in full, and because the five praises are numerous, they are not included here.
Each person, kneeling with devotion, offered one verse and one prostration.
Once the ritual bathing and offerings were fully completed,
the ācārya took the scented water used for bathing the Buddha.
Drip from the crown of the head and sprinkle upon the heads of the great assembly;
this is the auspicious water of merit and virtue, adorned with the myriad qualities of all the holy ones.
Let it moisten your bodies and drink of it in small or large measure.
It can cause the afflictions within one's body to diminish and thin away,
gradually leading to the accomplishment of unsurpassed bodhi.
The great assembly simultaneously paid homage with sincere devotion.
Then, further blowing the conch shells and chanting the *Pranidhāna-gāthā*, the *Maṅgala-gāthā*, and other hymns,
with the sounds of stringed and wind instruments leading the assembly forward,
they circumambulate the sacred object three or seven times, moving counter-clockwise according to the direction of the sun, following the proper order of rank from superior to inferior.
According to their respective inclinations, each person shall recite sublime verses from the Mahāyāna sūtras in praise of the Buddha.
Once the ritual service is completed, they shall prostrate and take leave of the Buddha;
then, individuals shall carry one image each back to its original location.
This is the constant ritual for bathing images in the West;
only thereafter do the assembly of monks ascend the hall to receive their food.
Alas, how tragic! In this land, there is no one who knows this.
Furthermore, the Buddha image had never been bathed once during its entire lifetime;
it was blackened by smoke, covered in dust, and defiled by crows, rats, and filth.
This was the case throughout the entire kingdom, and no one was able to understand why.
If there are those who bathe, following the foolish customs of their ancestors,
they fashion a separate image of the Buddha in the nude and place it within the water vessel,
washing it with a small ladle.
If one offers [the offering] with a haughty mind, utterly devoid of reverence, it will instead incur the fault of being treated with contempt. Alas!
One does not realize the greatness of the merit found in the field of respect.
High-sighted gentlemen, wise and sagacious persons,
and those who fear transgression while seeking merit—
such as these should especially take heed of this Dharma.
Even for those who cannot bathe every day,
it is also appropriate to do so once a month.
The extraordinary benefits obtained are as spoken from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata in the *Bathing the Image Sūtra*.
